calc.title:
Translate your life
into one number
calc.lede: Every amount is in today’s purchasing power. Not sure? That is fine — each field comes with a plain-language explanation and real-world anchors. Take your time. This may be the most worthwhile arithmetic you do today.
calc.groupLifeDesc: At what standard of living would you stop working for money?
calc.monthlyHelp: Rent, food, transport, travel, fun — in today’s prices, excluding children, a home purchase and major medical costs.
calc.kidsHelp: From planning a child to age 18, including education, health and care.
calc.healthHelp: For serious illness, care and later-life medical costs. Enter a household total.
calc.homeHelp: A dream home, a business, studying abroad — one-off items. If you rent, put rent in your monthly budget instead.
calc.groupBigDesc: Not monthly, but they can move your freedom threshold substantially.
calc.groupStartDesc: These do not change the number, but they decide how long it takes to get there.
calc.assetsHelp: Exclude your home, emergency fund and money needed soon.
calc.savingsHelp: What you can invest consistently after payday.
calc.ageHelp: Used to estimate the age you reach freedom.
calc.returnHelp: After inflation. The video uses 2.5%, which gives 480×. History does not guarantee the future.
calc.multiplierNote: Multiplier = 12 ÷ real return. The more optimistic the return, the less capital you need — and the more risk you carry.
calc.privacy: No uploads, no tracking. Every calculation happens in your browser.
calc.asideNote: The multiplier is not magic. It is 12 ÷ real return: enough for your assets to pay for life, keep up with inflation and never run out.
calc.gaugeNote: The higher the multiplier, the more capital the same life requires.
calc.asideQuote: “Don’t overestimate the joy after financial freedom — or overlook the beauty in front of you.”
calc.tip.monthly:
A simple way to estimate
Open the last three months of statements. Add rent or mortgage, food, transport, insurance, travel and fun, then average them. Do not forget annual costs — divide them by 12 and add them in.
calc.tip.kids:
An anchor, not a standard
China’s 2024 fertility-cost report puts the national average cost of raising a child to 18 at about ¥580,000; Beijing around ¥1m and Shanghai about ¥1.08m. For multiple children, average cost is often about 15% lower per child; adjust if that fits you.
calc.tip.health:
A safety margin, not a forecast
China’s lifetime health spending per person averages roughly ¥200,000. A practical range is ¥150k–300k per person in a tier-2 city and ¥300k–600k in a tier-1 city. Family history, insurance and age all matter.
calc.tip.home:
Buying and renting: choose one method
Buying: put the full price, or the deposit plus mortgage principal you will actually pay, here. Renting: put monthly rent in your life budget and do not double count it.
calc.tip.return:
Why 2.5% by default?
A 4%–4.5% nominal return minus 2% inflation leaves about 2%–2.5% real. At 2.5%, the multiplier is 480×. At 3%, it falls to 400×; at 2%, it rises to 600×. The more optimistic the assumption, the more you should ask: why me, why now?

method.title:
Freedom is not a guess.
It has four variables
method.lede: This formula does not promise wealth. It turns “how much do I need?” from anxiety into a question you can break down, act on and revisit.

method.cards.label: LIFESTYLE
method.cards.title: Monthly life × 480
method.cards.body: This is the spine. At a 2.5% real return, 480 represents the months of life your capital must cover while you spend one month each month and still keep pace with inflation.

method.cards.label: CHILDREN
method.cards.title: Children × cost per child
method.cards.body: Raising a child is not a fixed monthly bill. It is a large, 18-year commitment. Estimate the total cost from planning to adulthood, then multiply by the number of children.

method.cards.label: HEALTH
method.cards.title: Lifetime health reserve
method.cards.body: Medical costs are wildly uncertain. This is not money you expect to spend; it is the buffer that stops one illness from breaking the whole plan.

method.cards.label: CAPITAL
method.cards.title: Home and other big items
method.cards.body: A home, a business, study abroad, caring for parents — one-off capital does not fit the 480× logic. Add it directly. If you rent, keep rent in your monthly budget.

method.deepCaption:
One month of life,
multiplied by 480 months
method.deepLede: The video uses a deliberately conservative real-return assumption: 4%–4.5% nominal, about 2% long-run inflation, leaving roughly 2.5% real. Twelve months divided by 2.5% gives 480.

method.points.body: There are 12 months in a year. To make your capital produce 12 months of life every year, start with your annual spending.
After inflation, your money still has to work. This is the long-run, conservative assumption used in the video — not a guarantee.
12 ÷ 2.5% = 480. Not magic: a ruler. The lower the real return, the more capital you need.

method.deepNote: Note: the 4% rule usually estimates a withdrawal rate that spends down the portfolio over time. 480× is stricter: the principal must not shrink, and purchasing power must not fall.

method.assumptions.title: Inflation never stops
method.assumptions.body: At 2% inflation, $10,000 of purchasing power becomes about $6,700 in 20 years. The formula uses a real return, so this erosion is already removed.

method.assumptions.title: Returns are not a straight line
method.assumptions.body: Markets fluctuate. A bad early sequence can hurt even if the average return is fine. Keep one to two years of living costs as a buffer.

method.assumptions.title: Life will change the answer
method.assumptions.body: Partnership, children, moving, caring for parents — all change your monthly life. Recalculate every year or two. Iteration beats false precision.

method.assumptions.title: This is not permission to lie flat
method.assumptions.body: Financial freedom does not buy “doing nothing”. It buys the ability to say no. Do not miss the life in front of you for a number.

quote.text: Don’t overestimate the joy after financial freedom. Don’t overlook the beauty in front of you.
quote.by: Freedom is not splitting life into suffering now and pleasure later. It is having a choice again.
guide.title:
Before you fill it in,
understand it
guide.lede: No finance degree required. Read these notes and your estimate of freedom will be clearer than most.

guide.items.title: Where does 480 actually come from?
body: The core assumption: 4%–4.5% nominal return, 2% long-run inflation, which leaves about 2.5% real. If you spend x a month, you spend 12x a year. To earn 12x in real terms without shrinking capital, you need 12x ÷ 2.5% = 480x.

Another way to say it: every 480 units of capital can permanently support 1 unit of monthly spending. Spend 1,000 more a month, and your threshold rises by 480,000. The multiplier translates “how I want to live” into “how much capital I need”.

This differs from the familiar 4% rule. The 4% rule usually allows the portfolio to be spent down; 480× requires both principal and purchasing power to survive. It is more conservative, and better suited to the extreme assumption of never working again.
guide.items.aside: 480× is the result of a 2.5% real return, not a law of the universe.

guide.items.title: How should I estimate monthly life?
body: Do not start with “what should I spend?” Start with “how do I want to live?” If you stopped working tomorrow, what would an ordinary month look like: where would you live, what would you eat, how would you move, how often would you travel, would you pay for help?
The costs most often missed are non-monthly: insurance, health checks, gifts, replacing devices, home repairs. Add the last 12 months and divide by 12. That is usually more honest than a guess.
If you plan to rent forever, include rent in monthly life. If you plan to buy, put the purchase in major capital. Do not count both.
guide.items.aside: China’s 2025 average household consumption is about ¥2,456 per person per month.

guide.items.title: How much should I reserve for children?
body: China’s fertility-cost report estimates an average of about ¥580,000 to raise a child from planning to age 18 in 2024. Beijing is around ¥1m, Shanghai about ¥1.08m, Guizhou about ¥430,000. Regional differences are huge.
This is not one payment. It is spread across 18 years. In the freedom number, we reserve it upfront so future cash flow is not broken by it.

For multiple children, you can lower the per-child cost: the report suggests roughly 15% lower average cost for each additional child. Education choices matter even more — public versus international can be a different order of magnitude.
guide.items.aside: This only covers age 18. University and a first home are extra.

guide.items.title: Why can’t I skip the health reserve?
body: China’s official lifetime health spending averages about ¥200,000 per person, but that measure is narrow. A more practical range: ¥150k–300k per person in a tier-2 city, ¥300k–600k in a tier-1 city, adjusted for family history, age and insurance.
Health money behaves differently. You may never use it, or one illness may consume it in a year. It should not chase high returns; it belongs somewhere liquid and low-risk.
If you have private medical insurance, this reserve can focus on what insurance does not cover: self-paid drugs, care, lost income and treatment abroad.
guide.items.aside: Better to hold a little extra than to sell assets at the worst moment.

guide.items.title: How do housing, rent and pensions fit?
body: Buying: put the full price, or the deposit plus mortgage principal you will actually pay, into major capital. It does not get the 480× compounding treatment; it is added directly to the target.
Renting: put monthly rent into monthly life. It is then covered by the 480× multiplier automatically, because rent is an ongoing living cost, not one-off capital.

Pensions and social security: the formula assumes you are entirely self-funded. If you will have a reliable pension, you can lower the target modestly — but do not bank all of it on an uncertain system decades away.
guide.items.aside: Buying and renting: use only one method.

guide.items.title: Why can’t I just assume a higher return?
body: Move the return from 2.5% to 3.5% and the multiplier falls from 480 to about 343; your freedom number drops by nearly 30%. That is why optimistic assumptions are dangerous: they make the target look closer without changing the risk.
The video uses 2.5% because, after 2% inflation, it only requires a 4%–4.5% nominal return. For most people that already demands a sensible asset allocation, not a savings account.
The safer move is a stress test: recalculate at 2%. If that number feels impossible, the answer is probably to adjust spending or income, not to invent a better return.
guide.items.aside: Recalculate at a lower return. Does the plan still hold?

faq.title:
A few
honest questions
faq.lede: If you still have questions, you are taking your life seriously.

faq.items.a: No. It is a ruler customised to your life. Change the city, your spending habits or the return assumption and the number changes. Its value is not precision; it is making trade-offs visible.

faq.items.q: How is 480× different from the 4% rule?
faq.items.a: The 4% rule usually means withdrawing 4% a year and allowing the principal to run out after about 30 years. 480× requires the principal never to shrink and purchasing power never to fall. The assumptions differ; do not mix them.

faq.items.q: I own a home / have no children. What do I enter?
faq.items.a: If you own a home you do not plan to replace, enter 0 for major capital. If you have a mortgage, put the monthly payment in living costs. With no children, set the count to 0 and the childcare term becomes zero.
You can, but be conservative. Subtract the present value of a reliable pension from the target, or reduce the target by 10%–20%. Do not assume the system will be unchanged decades from now.

faq.items.q: Why is my number so much higher than my friend’s?
faq.items.a: Because your living costs, children, health reserve and housing plans differ. Financial freedom is not a competition. It is only about the life you want.
No. Every calculation, chart and share card is generated in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server when you refresh or close the page.

plan.title: Your long-term savings plan
plan.lede: From today to freedom, how compounding takes the baton.
plan.chartHint: All amounts in today’s purchasing power
plan.note: Assumes monthly contributions rise with inflation, stable returns and no extra large withdrawals. Real markets fluctuate; keep a margin of safety.
plan.phasesSub: Turn the number into something you can do today

plan.phases.title: Build the floor
plan.phases.body: Save six months of living costs as an emergency fund and clear high-interest debt. Make the plan hard to break.

plan.phases.title: Let compounding accelerate
plan.phases.body: Automate monthly investing and build a diversified stock-and-bond portfolio. Each raise, add part of it to the plan.

plan.phases.title: Protect the result
plan.phases.body: As you approach the target, reduce volatility and hold one to two years of living costs as a buffer. Keep learning after freedom.

plan.accelHint: Saving 20% more each month gets you there {years} years earlier.
plan.accelZero: Saving 20% more barely changes the date. Consider investing more or lowering the target.
plan.notReached: Under these assumptions, you will not arrive within 60 years. Try increasing monthly investing.
